title: Tension Index: Europe
notice: An indicator of escalation signals (0–10) from governments' travel advice, aviation, news and markets. Not a forecast and not advice to leave.
hint: Select a country for details. Zoom with two fingers or the +/− buttons. Link to a country: …/dashboard/#PL

method: Six signal blocks (government advice and embassy posture, aviation, domestic measures, aggressor signals, media, markets) combine as independent confirmations. What counts: the stated reason, the number of independent sources, governments acting in sync, and deviation from the country's usual level. Decisive events (embassy staff departure, airspace closure, mobilisation) guarantee a minimum score. Weights are a starting hypothesis, tested on historical episodes.
empty: No data yet: the dashboard fills in after the first scoring run.
ctxNote: Not scored: the index covers 38 European countries and shows escalation signals where there is no war yet. Neighbours are shown for context.

mean.green: Usual background: sources show no signs of escalation, or only routine edits.
mean.yellow: Isolated changes worth watching, but they do not yet add up to a pattern.
mean.orange: Several independent signals at once, or one strong signal in a key block.
mean.red: Strong signals: embassy staff departure, airspace closure, or several governments raising their advice together.
mean.critical: Decisive events: ordered staff departure by several governments, mobilisation, airspace closure.

quiet: No block shows warning signals: every source is at its usual background.
floorHit: A threshold event occurred, so the score is not below the minimum set for it.
notForecast: This describes what the sources show now; it is not a probability or a forecast.

flagText.short_history: Less than 30 days of observations, so comparison with the country's usual level is not applied yet.
flagText.low_coverage: Fresh data from fewer than half of the blocks: no score is published (except threshold events).
flagText.synchrony: Several governments ({n}) tightened their advice within a week: the score is multiplied by 1.2.
flagText.isolated: Rising in this country only while neighbours are calm: possibly a local cause.
flagText.regional_escalation: Rising in most neighbouring countries at once: a regional escalation.

advisories: Travel advice levels from the US, UK, Germany, Canada and France, and their embassies' posture (authorized or ordered staff departure).
aviation: EASA conflict zone bulletins, airspace closures or restrictions, sharp drops in air traffic from OpenSky data.
domestic: Mobilisation, state of emergency, border closures.
aggressor: Russian or Belarusian foreign ministry telling its citizens to avoid the country, direct threats, hybrid attacks (drones, sabotage, GPS jamming).
media: Escalation news confirmed by at least two outlets, and surges of military-related coverage (GDELT).
markets: Government bond spread jumps and currency drops (ECB data).

methodFull: What it is and isn't

The Tension Index shows how many escalation signals are currently visible in open sources for each of 38 European countries, on a 0–10 scale. It is a state indicator, not a probability of war and not a forecast. A high score means “many sources are raising alarms at once”, not “a war will start”.
The score is not advice to leave or to stay. For decisions, follow your own government's official travel advice.
Scale levels
LEVELS
Six blocks
BLOCKS
How blocks combine

Each block gets a value from 0 to 100%. Every block has a cap (government advice, aviation and domestic measures up to 60%, aggressor signals 40%, media 35%, markets 15%): one block, even fully alarmed, cannot produce the maximum score. Blocks combine as independent confirmations: each further alarmed block moves the total towards the maximum but never adds more than what is left.

Within a block one publisher counts once (its strongest signal), while different publishers reinforce each other. For EU and NATO members, government advice weighs a quarter less: allies rarely raise each other's danger level in advance.

One-off events (advice updates, news, traffic drops) fade over time, while states (the current advice level, a closed airspace) hold while they last. The total becomes a 0–10 score through a curve that stretches the low end of the scale so early, moderate signals are visible.
Threshold events
Some events guarantee a minimum score on their own, to keep the scale interpretable:
• authorized departure of embassy staff by at least one government: at least 7;
• ordered departure or embassy closure by at least two governments: at least 9;
• mobilisation: at least 9;
• airspace closed, reported by at least two independent sources: at least 8; restricted: at least 6.
Flags

“Short history”: under 30 days of data, comparison with the country's norm is off. “Synchrony”: three or more governments tightened their advice within a week (score ×1.2). “This country only”: neighbours are calm. “Regional escalation”: most neighbours are rising. With fresh data from fewer than half of the blocks, no score is published (except threshold events).
Limitations

Governments update their advice late and for political reasons. News and traffic data are noisy, so a single source rarely produces a high score. The weights are a starting hypothesis, tested on historical episodes (Ukraine 2022, Armenia and Azerbaijan 2020, Israel 2024). Countries are checked from hourly to every 12 hours: the higher the score, the more often; media (GDELT) once a day.

stab.title: Government and security forces
stab.desc: From the country's national media: decisions favouring the aggressor, security chiefs removed or arrested, armed men without insignia, the leader's disappearance, violent unrest, falling trust. 0 means no such signals. It describes what is reported, not a forecast.
stab.none: No such signals in the last 30 days.

cat.armed_unmarked: Armed men without insignia, attacks by people in uniform
